### Problem: Minimum Number of Arrows to Burst Balloons {#sec-int-p4-a}

::: {.p-statement}
$n$ balloons are on the $x$-axis; balloon $i$ spans the closed interval $[x_{\text{start}, i}, x_{\text{end}, i}]$ ($1 \le n \le 10^5$, $-2^{31} \le x_{\text{start}} < x_{\text{end}} \le 2^{31} - 1$). An arrow shot at $x$ from below bursts every balloon with $x_{\text{start}} \le x \le x_{\text{end}}$ (touching the edge bursts it). Find the **minimum number of arrows** to burst all balloons.

Source: [LC 452 · Minimum Number of Arrows to Burst Balloons](https://leetcode.com/problems/minimum-number-of-arrows-to-burst-balloons/){.solved difficulty="Medium"}

Example: `[[10,16],[2,8],[1,6],[7,12]]` → $2$ (shoot at $x=6$ bursts $[1,6]$ and $[2,8]$; shoot at $x=12$ bursts $[10,16]$ and $[7,12]$).
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
This is @sec-int-sched's *stab* problem — the exact dual of maximum-independent-set on intervals. For intervals, the minimum number of points hitting every interval equals the maximum number of pairwise disjoint intervals: no point can hit two disjoint intervals, and the greedy below finds as many points as disjoint intervals. The greedy that reads off both is: **sort by end ascending, shoot at the smallest end that's still unburst; skip every balloon that shot bursts; recurse**. Exchange: any valid arrow set has to cover the balloon with the smallest end $b_{\min}$; the only positions that hit it are in $[a_{\min}, b_{\min}]$; sliding the covering arrow right to $b_{\min}$ itself can only *help* (nothing to the right of $b_{\min}$ loses coverage, and everything in $[a_{\min}, b_{\min}]$ that the original shot hit is still hit). So there is an optimal solution that shoots at $b_{\min}$ — remove every balloon it bursts, repeat.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
1. **Test endpoints, then minimum-subset-cover (oracle).** Any arrow can be slid right until it sits on the smallest right end among the balloons it bursts, without losing any of them. So some optimal set of arrows uses only right ends; enumerate subsets of the distinct right ends in increasing size until one bursts every balloon. Exponential in worst case but tiny on the trace example.
2. **Sort by start + chain intersection.** Sort by start ascending. Maintain the current *intersection window* $[\text{lo}, \text{hi}]$ — the range of $x$ values a single arrow can hit to burst every balloon in the current group. Extend with $[\max(\text{lo}, a), \min(\text{hi}, b)]$; when the window would go empty, spend a new arrow and start a fresh window. $O(n\log n)$.
3. **Sort by end + greedy shot (canonical).** Sort by end ascending. Set `shot` to negative infinity; for each balloon, if $a_i >$ `shot`, spend an arrow and set `shot` to $b_i$. Count shots. $O(n\log n)$, $O(1)$ extra state.

**Invariant.** After processing $k$ balloons in end-sorted order, `shot` is the end of the last arrow fired, and every one of the first $k$ balloons is burst by some arrow in the fired set. The chain-intersection form maintains the dual invariant: `[lo, hi]` is non-empty iff the current group can still share an arrow.
:::

The buttons are in order. Each one keeps the previous solution and changes only what that form changes.

::: {.panel-tabset .solution-forms}

#### Test endpoints, then minimum subset cover

::: {.form-next}
The oracle: some optimal set of arrows uses only right ends of balloons (slide each arrow right to the smallest right end among the balloons it bursts). Enumerate subsets of endpoints in increasing size until one covers every balloon. Exponential in principle ($2^m$ subsets of the $m \le n$ distinct right ends) but tiny on hand examples: our trace input has four right ends, so $2^4 = 16$ subsets in all.

**Worked example.** Balloons $[(10,16),(2,8),(1,6),(7,12)]$: endpoints $\{6, 8, 12, 16\}$. Single arrows cover at most $2$ balloons each. Try $\{6, 12\}$: covers $[1,6]$ (via $6$), $[2,8]$ (via $6$), $[7,12]$ (via $12$), $[10,16]$ (via $12$). All four burst → answer $2$.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
def arrows_brute(balloons):
    ends = sorted({b for _, b in balloons})
    for r in range(1, len(ends) + 1):
        for combo in itertools.combinations(ends, r):
            if all(any(a <= x <= b for x in combo) for a, b in balloons):
                return r
    return len(balloons)
```

##### C++

```cpp
// fragment - brute force oracle over endpoint subsets
#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>
#include <set>
using namespace std;
int arrowsBrute(vector<vector<int>>& balloons) {
    set<int> s;
    for (auto& b : balloons) s.insert(b[1]);
    vector<int> ends(s.begin(), s.end());
    int m = (int)ends.size();
    for (int mask = 1; mask < (1 << m); ++mask) {
        bool ok = true;
        for (auto& bl : balloons) {
            bool hit = false;
            for (int j = 0; j < m; ++j)
                if ((mask & (1 << j)) && ends[j] >= bl[0] && ends[j] <= bl[1]) { hit = true; break; }
            if (!hit) { ok = false; break; }
        }
        if (ok) return __builtin_popcount(mask);
    }
    return (int)balloons.size();
}
```
:::

**Reading it line by line.** Enumerating subsets of the *endpoints* (not of all real numbers!) is the correctness reduction from the exchange argument. Python's `itertools.combinations(ends, r)` walks them in lex order; the outer loop increasing $r$ means the first hit is a minimum. The C++ bitmask form tops out at $m \le 20$ or so — practical only for tiny inputs — and is present as the oracle the two fast forms are measured against.

#### Sort by start + chain intersection

::: {.form-next}
Sort by start ascending. Maintain a *window* $[\text{lo}, \text{hi}]$: the range of $x$ values that burst every balloon in the current group with one arrow. For a new balloon $(a, b)$: if $a > $ `hi`, the groups can't share an arrow → spend a new arrow with `lo=a, hi=b`; else tighten the window to $[\max(\text{lo}, a), \min(\text{hi}, b)]$. Count of arrows spent is the answer. $O(n\log n)$ time, $O(1)$ extra state.

**Worked example.** Sorted by start $[(1,6),(2,8),(7,12),(10,16)]$. Start: `lo=1, hi=6, arrows=1`. See $(2,8)$: $2 \le 6$, tighten to $[2, 6]$. See $(7,12)$: $7 > 6$, spend arrow → `lo=7, hi=12, arrows=2`. See $(10,16)$: $10 \le 12$, tighten to $[10, 12]$. **Total $=2$**.
:::

##### Python

```{python}
#| label: arr-0452-chain
def arrows_chain(balloons):
    if not balloons:
        return 0
    s = sorted(balloons)
    lo, hi = s[0]
    arrows = 1
    for a, b in s[1:]:
        if a > hi:                                # disjoint: new arrow
            arrows += 1
            lo, hi = a, b
        else:                                     # overlap: tighten window
            lo = max(lo, a)
            hi = min(hi, b)
    return arrows

for _ in range(300):
    n = random.randint(1, 8)
    balloons = []
    for _ in range(n):
        a = random.randint(-10, 10); b = a + random.randint(1, 6)
        balloons.append((a, b))
    assert arrows_chain(balloons) == arrows_brute(balloons)
assert arrows_chain([[10,16],[2,8],[1,6],[7,12]]) == 2   # LC sample
assert arrows_chain([[1,2],[3,4],[5,6],[7,8]]) == 4      # all disjoint
assert arrows_chain([[1,2],[2,3]]) == 1                  # touching: closed convention
print("arrows_chain OK")
```

##### C++

```cpp
#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>
using namespace std;
int arrowsChain(vector<vector<int>> balloons) {
    if (balloons.empty()) return 0;
    sort(balloons.begin(), balloons.end());
    int lo = balloons[0][0], hi = balloons[0][1], arrows = 1;
    for (size_t i = 1; i < balloons.size(); ++i) {
        int a = balloons[i][0], b = balloons[i][1];
        if (a > hi) { ++arrows; lo = a; hi = b; }
        else { lo = max(lo, a); hi = min(hi, b); }
    }
    return arrows;
}

int main() {
    vector<vector<int>> v{{10,16},{2,8},{1,6},{7,12}};
    arrowsChain(v);
}
```
:::

**Reading it line by line.** `a > hi` (strict) is the closed-interval convention: a balloon starting exactly at the current window's right edge $x = $ `hi` can still share the arrow (shoot at `hi`; both balloons contain that point). Flip to `a >= hi` and you'll spend an extra arrow on $[1,3],[3,5]$. The tighten step is where the *real* insight lives: after processing the prefix, `hi` can only decrease (each intersection takes `min` with a new $b$), and `lo` can only increase — so the window never grows. When it goes empty we start a new group.

#### Sort by end + greedy shot

::: {.form-next}
The canonical answer and by far the shortest to code. Sort by **end** ascending. Walk with `shot` starting at negative infinity; if $a_i >$ `shot`, spend a new arrow at $b_i$ and update `shot` to $b_i$. Balloons with $a_i \le$ `shot` are already burst by the current shot and are skipped. $O(n\log n)$ time, $O(1)$ extra state.

**Worked example.** Sorted by end $[(1,6),(2,8),(7,12),(10,16)]$: shot $= -\infty$; see $(1,6)$: $1 > -\infty$ → new arrow at $6$, count $1$; see $(2,8)$: $2 \le 6$ skip; see $(7,12)$: $7 > 6$ → new arrow at $12$, count $2$; see $(10,16)$: $10 \le 12$ skip. **Total $=2$**.
:::

##### Python

```{python}
#| label: arr-0452-optimal
def arrows_optimal(balloons):
    if not balloons:
        return 0
    s = sorted(balloons, key=lambda x: x[1])
    shot = -math.inf
    arrows = 0
    for a, b in s:
        if a > shot:                       # this balloon survived every arrow so far
            arrows += 1
            shot = b                       # shoot at its end - optimal by exchange
    return arrows

for _ in range(300):
    n = random.randint(1, 8)
    balloons = []
    for _ in range(n):
        a = random.randint(-10, 10); b = a + random.randint(1, 6)
        balloons.append((a, b))
    assert arrows_optimal(balloons) == arrows_brute(balloons)
    assert arrows_optimal(balloons) == arrows_chain(balloons)
assert arrows_optimal([[10,16],[2,8],[1,6],[7,12]]) == 2
assert arrows_optimal([[1,2],[2,3],[3,4]]) == 2       # chain: [1,2],[2,3] share; [3,4] alone
print("arrows_optimal OK")
```

##### C++

```cpp
#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>
#include <climits>
using namespace std;
int arrowsOptimal(vector<vector<int>> balloons) {
    if (balloons.empty()) return 0;
    sort(balloons.begin(), balloons.end(),
         [](auto& x, auto& y) { return x[1] < y[1]; });
    long long shot = LLONG_MIN;
    int arrows = 0;
    for (auto& bl : balloons) {
        if (bl[0] > shot) { ++arrows; shot = bl[1]; }
    }
    return arrows;
}

int main() {
    vector<vector<int>> v{{10,16},{2,8},{1,6},{7,12}};
    arrowsOptimal(v);
}
```
:::

**Reading it line by line.** Two facts drive the whole algorithm: **sort by end**, and **only check `a_i > shot`**. The comparison is strict because closed intervals: a balloon starting exactly at `shot` is already burst by an arrow at `shot` (touching the edge). The C++ version uses `long long` and `LLONG_MIN` for the initial `shot` because coordinates reach $-2^{31}$, the smallest `int`: no `int` sentinel lies strictly below every start. The same range is why comparators must compare (`x[1] < y[1]`) and never subtract (`x[1] - y[1]` overflows). The three-line greedy is the *fastest* to code in an interview; the chain form (rung 2) is a *different* correct greedy with the same complexity, useful when the interviewer asks "can you do it sorted by start?".
:::

::: {.p-complexity}
**Endpoint-subset brute** is $O(2^{m} \cdot n \cdot m)$ with $m \le 2n$ distinct endpoints — the oracle. **Chain intersection** and **sort-by-end greedy** are both $O(n\log n)$ time, $O(1)$ extra space beyond the sort. The greedy form has smaller constants (no `min`/`max` in the loop) and shorter code; either passes LC's $n \le 10^5$.
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- **Two balloons touching at a point** $[1,3], [3,5]$: closed convention means one arrow at $x=3$ bursts both. Every fast form returns $1$.
- **Nested balloons** $[1,10], [2,3], [4,5]$: sort by end gives $[(2,3),(4,5),(1,10)]$; shoot at $3$, shoot at $5$; skip $(1,10)$ (its start $1 \le 5$). Answer $2$.
- **Extreme coordinates**: $x_{\text{start}}$ can be $-2^{31}$. Use `-math.inf` (Python) or a `long long` sentinel (C++), and never sort with a subtracting comparator.
- **$n = 1$**: one arrow. Handled by the empty-check + first-iteration branch.
- **All balloons identical**: one arrow. Sort by end gives any order; the first shot at $b$ covers every subsequent $a \le$ `shot`.
:::
